COMPULSORY ELECTIVE AREA 3 · MAY

Surveying problems

How tall is the tree in the school yard? How wide is the pond? With a home-made forester’s triangle, a measuring wheel, your own thumb and a little trigonometry, you survey the area around your school – just like land surveyors, only with simpler tools. At the end comes a presentation of your results.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSOUTDOORSPRESENTATION
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • know, build and use surveying tools: forester’s triangle, measuring wheel, sighting stick
  • find heights and distances with similar triangles, Pythagoras’ theorem and trigonometry
  • draw measurements to scale and round them sensibly
  • plan, carry out and present a survey

EXPLORATIONSTO GET STARTED · IN GROUPS
BUILDING THE FORESTER’S TRIANGLE

Cut an isosceles right-angled triangle with legs of 20 cm out of stiff card. Hang a plumb line made of thread and a nut from one corner.

  • Sight the top of a tree along the hypotenuse and hold one leg vertical with the plumb line. Walk forwards or backwards until it fits. What is true then?
→ Unit 1
THE THUMB JUMP

Stretch out your arm and sight a house over your thumb with one eye. Switch eyes: the thumb jumps.

  • Measure the length of your arm and the distance between your eyes. How can you use them to estimate the distance to the house?
→ Unit 1
UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Surveying tools

When the sighting with the forester’s triangle fits, the angle to the top of the tree is exactly $45^\circ$. Then the height of the tree above your eyes is the same as your distance from the trunk. You measure that with a tape measure or a measuring wheel, and add your eye level.

KEY POINT · SURVEYING WITH SIMPLE MEANS

Forester’s triangle ($45^\circ$): height = distance + eye level.

Shadow method, sighting stick, thumb jump: similar triangles, so equal ratios (intercept theorem).

Angle of elevation $\alpha$ from the distance $d$: height = $d \cdot \tan \alpha$ + eye level.

Measuring wheel: distance = number of turns times circumference.

A right angle without a set square: a string with 12 equal sections, stretched into 3, 4 and 5 sections, gives a right angle.

Angle app: many smartphones measure angles of inclination. Hold the device steady along the edge of the screen while sighting.

INTERACTIVE · SHADOW METHOD AND FORESTER’S TRIANGLE

Choose the method. With the shadow method you compare the stick and the tree, with the forester’s triangle you walk back until the sighting fits.

EXAMPLE 1 · WITH THE FORESTER’S TRIANGLE

The sighting fits 18 m from the trunk, the eyes are 1.6 m high. How tall is the tree?

$18 + 1.6 =$ 19.6 m

EXAMPLE 2 · THE THUMB JUMP

Arm 60 cm, distance between the eyes 6 cm. In front of a house the thumb seems to jump by 30 m. How far away is the house?

Ratio $60 \div 6 = 10$, the same holds outside: distance $\approx 10 \cdot 30 =$ 300 m.

EXERCISES

A measuring wheel has a circumference of 1 m and turns 245 times. How long is the path? What is the diameter of the wheel?

245 m. $d = \tfrac{1}{\pi} \approx 31.8$ cm.

A stick 1 m long casts a shadow of 1.25 m, a building at the same time one of 15 m. How tall is the building?

$15 \div 1.25 = 12$ m

From a distance of 25 m an app measures the angle of elevation $38^\circ$ to the top of a mast, eye level 1.5 m. How tall is the mast?

$25 \cdot \tan 38^\circ + 1.5 \approx 21.0$ m

A stick 2 m tall stands 4 m in front of you. When you lie with your eye on the ground, the top of the stick and the top of the tower are in line. The tower is 40 m away. How tall is it?

$\tfrac{h}{40} = \tfrac24$, so $h = 20$ m.

20 paces measure 15 m. For the path round the school yard you need 280 paces. How long is it? How accurate is the result if each pace can vary by 5 cm?

Length of a pace 0.75 m, path 210 m. With ±5 cm per pace at most $\pm 14$ m – in reality less, because the deviations partly cancel out.

$15 \div 1.25$

Height of the mast from exercise 3, to one decimal place?

$19.5 + 1.5$

UNIT 2PROJECT · 4 LESSONS

2Surveying around the school

You cannot simply cross a pond with a tape measure. But you can stake out a baseline on the bank, measure its length and from both ends find the angles to a point on the other bank. The sine rule does the rest – just as in a great national survey.

KEY POINT · CARRYING OUT A SURVEY

Plan: what is to be measured? Which method, which tools? A sketch with all the known and unknown quantities.

Measure: every measurement several times, take the mean. Check outliers and repeat them.

Evaluate: calculate, draw to scale, round to the accuracy of the measurements.

Present: sketch, measurements, calculation, result with unit, sources of error.

Rounding sensibly: if the measurements are accurate to 0.1 m, a result such as 17.7634 m is spurious precision. The right answer is 17.8 m.

TOOL · TRIANGLE SOLVER

Enter the measured parts: the baseline and two angles. The solver calculates the other sides for checking.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE POND

Baseline $AB = 50$ m, angle at $A$ $75^\circ$, at $B$ $65^\circ$ to a point $C$ on the other bank. How far is $C$ from $A$?

Angle at $C$: $40^\circ$. $AC = \tfrac{50 \cdot \sin 65^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} \approx$ 70.5 m.

EXAMPLE 4 · TWO ANGLES, NO ACCESS

The foot of a tower cannot be reached. From $A$ you see the top at $30^\circ$, 20 m closer (at $B$) at $45^\circ$. How tall is the tower above eye level?

At $B$: $h = d$. At $A$: $h = (d + 20) \tan 30^\circ$. From this $d \approx 27.3$ m, so $h \approx 27.3$ m.

EXERCISES

A school yard measures 60 m × 45 m. How long is the diagonal, how large is the area? How long is the diagonal on a plan at the scale 1 : 500?

75 m, $2700\,\text{m}^2$, 15 cm on the plan.

Four groups measure the same distance: 12.4 m, 12.6 m, 12.5 m and 12.9 m. Give the mean.

$50.4 \div 4 = 12.6$ m

You stake out a corner: 6 m along the wall, 8 m along the fence, the diagonal measures 10.2 m. Is the corner a right angle? Calculate the angle.

Not quite: $\cos \gamma = \tfrac{36 + 64 - 104.04}{96} \approx -0.042$, $\gamma \approx 92.4^\circ$.

A staircase has 15 steps, each 17 cm high and 29 cm deep. What difference in height does it overcome, how steep is it?

2.55 m. $\tan \alpha = \tfrac{17}{29}$, $\alpha \approx 30.4^\circ$.

In groups, plan a survey of your own at your school: the height of the school building, the width of the sports ground or the area of the school garden. Draw up a measuring plan and a presentation.

Assessed are: a sensible method, a neat sketch, several measurements with a mean, a calculation that can be followed, a sensibly rounded result, the sources of error named.

TEST YOURSELF!

$50 \cdot \sin 65^\circ \div \sin 40^\circ$

Height of the tower above eye level in example 4, to one decimal place?

$d = \tfrac{20 \tan 30^\circ}{1 - \tan 30^\circ}$

Mean of the measurements in exercise 7?

$50.4 \div 4$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A person 1.80 m tall casts a shadow of 2.40 m, a flagpole one of 16 m. How tall is the pole?

$16 \cdot 0.75 = 12$ m

When levelling, you read 1.85 m on the staff behind you and 0.60 m in front. How large is the difference in height, which point is higher? How large is the gradient over 50 m?

1.25 m, the front is higher. Gradient $1.25 \div 50 = 2.5\%$.

A ramp at the school entrance rises 0.25 m over 3 m. How large are the gradient and the angle of slope? For wheelchairs, at most 6% applies. Is the ramp suitable?

$8.3\%$, $\alpha \approx 4.8^\circ$. No, it is too steep.

Connecting with learning area 1: a triangular plot of land has the sides 40 m and 55 m with $68^\circ$ between them. Calculate the third side and the area.

$c^2 = 1600 + 3025 - 4400 \cos 68^\circ \approx 2976.7$, $c \approx 54.6$ m. Area $\approx 1019.9\,\text{m}^2$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Thales measures the pyramid

The Greek scholar Thales of Miletus is said to have found the height of an Egyptian pyramid in the 6th century BC without climbing up it. He waited for the time of day at which his own shadow was exactly as long as he was tall. At that moment, he reasoned, the shadow of the pyramid is also as long as its height.

That is the shadow method from this chapter in its simplest form: the sun’s rays are parallel, and the triangles made of height and shadow are similar.

Source: Diogenes Laertius: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers, book I, 27.
